The sea stretched in every direction, and the captain sat in a small open boat. He had no ship and no map of the way home. Around him sat eighteen men, thin and tired. The sun beat down on every one of them. Their ship, HMS Bounty, was gone. Hours earlier, some of its own crew had taken it away. Go back a little, to the end of seventeen eighty-seven. The Bounty sailed out of England carrying a special cargo: breadfruit trees. Breadfruit is a large fruit that can feed many people. Owners of farms in the Caribbean hoped to grow the trees there, to feed their workers cheaply. Bligh had orders to bring the plants safely home. The captain was William Bligh, a sailor who had once served under the famous explorer James Cook. Bligh was a skilled navigator, but many found him harsh. He often punished sailors with the lash, a whip used on the back. The ship reached Tahiti in October seventeen eighty-eight. Its crew loved the warm islands, and the Tahitian people welcomed the sailors warmly. The men stayed for five months, and many seemed sad when it was time to leave. Among the officers was Fletcher Christian, a young man whom Bligh had trusted. Why Christian rose against his captain is still debated. Some think he simply wanted to stay in Tahiti. People say he could no longer bear Bligh's anger. On the morning of April twenty-eighth, seventeen eighty-nine, Christian and his armed men seized the ship. They tied Bligh's hands and brought him up on deck. Christian became the new leader of the ship. Bligh and eighteen men were put into the launch, a small open boat towed behind the ship. They were given some food, some water, a compass, and a few tools. Then the Bounty sailed away, and the little boat was alone. Bligh was a brilliant navigator, and now he had to use every skill he had. He led the men across thousands of miles of open sea. They traveled about three thousand six hundred miles. Bligh kept a careful log of every day and every mile. Water was measured out with great care. Each man received only a very small portion of food. Some were sick, and some grew weak. After forty-seven days, the launch reached the town of Kupang on the island of Timor. Every man had survived, which was a remarkable thing. Bligh sailed home to England and told his story. He later returned to the Pacific with another ship and captured some of the mutineers. Meanwhile, Christian and a group of mutineers had sailed to a small, faraway island called Pitcairn. There they burned the Bounty. Their descendants still live on Pitcairn today. Bligh later became governor of New South Wales, a colony in Australia, where he faced a rebellion of his own. The captain got home, and the mutineers got an island that their great-grandchildren still call home.
